processing: Black tea graded by leaf size into Pekoe, Orange Pekoe and Broken Leaf; the factory also works as a museum of the island's tea making.
harvest_season: Picking begins in spring, which the factory marks each year with a recreated picking ritual; exact dates are not published.
appearance_dry: Dark leaf, with size set by grade: Pekoe is shorter than Orange Pekoe, and Broken Leaf is finest.
appearance_liquor: Reddish amber, stronger in the Broken Leaf grade.
appearance_wet: Coppery brown leaf, as with most small-grade black teas.
taste_profile: Little is recorded about the taste of the grades in detail; as a rule for black tea, Orange Pekoe gives a lighter cup and Broken Leaf the fullest and briskest.

brewing.notes: Brewed Western style. Cut the time for Broken Leaf, which gives up its strength quickly.

vintage_note: Sold as current production without a harvest year, by grade, at the factory and through Azorean shops. There are no vintages to chase; buy fresh and drink within a year or two, as with other packaged black tea.
description:
Porto Formoso is one of only two tea factories working on São Miguel in the Azores, a rare place for tea in Europe. The Pekoe is one of the grades of black tea it sells, alongside Orange Pekoe and Broken Leaf.

The grade names describe leaf size, not a different plant or a different method. That makes this row less a single recipe than a house style with three cuts, and little is published on the fine detail of how each is made.

Expect a straightforward black tea rather than something exotic. Brew it with water just off the boil, and shorten the steep for smaller leaf, since the broken grade turns strong fast.

The label is easily confused with its larger neighbour Gorreana, which sells grades with the same names. Check the factory name on the pack. The best way in is a visit: the tour ends with a tasting of several teas.
history:
Azorean tea has its roots in the 19th century. The Porto Formoso factory opened in the 1920s and closed in the 1980s, leaving Gorreana as the only one active.

It reopened in 2001 under new owners, and now combines production with a museum and guided visits. Some details of the timeline vary between accounts.
